name: Polygenic Risk Scores
title: Polygenic Risk Scores
answer: A polygenic risk score is a single number that sums the small effects of many common genetic variants linked to a disease. In genomic medicine it is used to place a person in a risk category relative to a reference population, not to diagnose disease. The score typically covers complex conditions such as coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, and breast cancer. It is one input among family history, biomarkers, and lifestyle factors in precision therapeutics.

In genomic medicine it is used to place a person in a risk category relative to a reference population, not to diagnose disease. The score typically covers complex conditions such as coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, and breast cancer. It is one input among family history, biomarkers, and lifestyle factors in precision therapeutics.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Polygenic risk scores are usually computed from genotype data produced by microarray chips that read hundreds of thousands to millions of single nucleotide polymorphisms. The underlying weights come from large genome wide association studies and biobank scale cohorts. Computation itself is lightweight, often a simple weighted sum that can run on a standard server or even a laptop. The heavier infrastructure is the secure storage and versioning of genotype data and reference panels.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with genome wide association study summary statistics that report the effect size of each variant on a trait. Variants are selected and weighted using methods such as clumping and thresholding or Bayesian shrinkage approaches like LDpred and PRS-CS. The score is then standardized against a population distribution so a patient's result can be reported as a percentile. Validation in independent cohorts is standard before any clinical use.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on genetic data privacy, consent, and the return of results to patients. Most scores perform worse in ancestry groups underrepresented in the original genome wide association studies, which can create inequitable risk estimates. Clinical validity and utility are still under review by regulators and professional bodies, and product liability questions remain open for scores sold directly to consumers or used in care. Provenance of the training data and the score version must be documented for any defensible clinical deployment.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward scores built from multiple ancestries and from whole genome sequencing rather than fixed microarrays. Researchers are combining polygenic scores with rare variant data, electronic health records, and other biomarkers to improve risk stratification. Clinical trials are testing whether score guided screening or prevention changes outcomes. Over time, scores may become a routine layer in health records, but their clinical adoption depends on closing the ancestry gap and proving utility in prospective studies.
